questions: Do you feel an uncomfortable sensation or an urge to move your legs before these movements occur?
Does moving your legs relieve that sensation or urge?
Do the movements occur mainly when you are sitting or lying still?
Are they worse in the evening or at night?
Can you voluntarily stop the movements briefly when you concentrate on doing so?
Do the movements continue while you are asleep?
Have they been occurring repeatedly in brief, highly similar episodes?
Do you remain fully aware and able to respond throughout each episode?
Have you ever lost awareness, stared blankly, bitten your tongue, or lost bladder control during them?
Do you have an inner feeling of being unable to keep still, beyond discomfort confined to your legs?
Have you recently started, stopped, or changed the dose of any medication?
Do you take an antipsychotic, antidepressant, nausea medication, stimulant, antihistamine, or medication for Parkinson’s disease?
Do the movements improve when you are distracted or become more noticeable when you focus on them?
Do you have weakness, numbness, tingling, or stiffness in either leg?
Do you have back pain or new difficulty controlling your bladder or bowels?
Have you had similar movements elsewhere in your body?
Has anyone in your family had similar movements or a diagnosed movement disorder?

results: 1. Comprehensive bedside neurological examination with testing for distractibility, entrainment, variability, and coherence of the movements
cranial nerve examination: normal
mental status / cognitive screen: normal
muscle tone examination: reduced tone in the left limbs
limb strength (MRC) examination: 5/5 throughout
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal reflexes and flexor plantar responses
sensory examination (pinprick, vibration, proprioception): normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): left-sided choreiform and ballistic movements; otherwise normal
posture and pull test: left-sided choreiform and ballistic movements; stable on pull test
fundoscopy: normal
distribution of the movements (one side, both, face, limbs): not characterised
effect of voluntary action and anxiety: no clear change
cognitive and behavioural assessment (MMSE / FAB): normal
speech assessment: normal
gait and coordination: normal
2. Prolonged video-EEG monitoring with simultaneous recording of the abnormal movements
EEG: normal
3. MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium contrast
MRI diffusion-weighted sequences: restricted diffusion consistent with a lacunar infarct
MRI susceptibility-weighted sequences: left striatal signal abnormality without hemorrhage
brain MRI with contrast: a coexisting LACUNAR INFARCT in addition to the striatal signal change
4. Serum glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, renal and liver function tests
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
liver function tests: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
blood glucose: 30.63 mmol/L (551.3 mg/dL) with glycosuria and NO ketonuria
renal function and eGFR: normal
5. Complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone, vitamin B12, and copper/ceruloplasmin levels
full blood count: normal
thyroid function (TSH, free T4): normal
vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid: normal
TSH, free T4 and free T3: normal
copper / caeruloplasmin: normal
6. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord with and without gadolinium contrast
MRI cervical and thoracic spine: normal

DIAGNOSIS: Nonketotic hyperglycemia–induced hemichorea–hemiballismus (diabetic striatopathy), with associated striatal MRI abnormality and a coexisting lacunar infarct

ALTERNATIVE: Lacunar infarct–induced hemichorea–hemiballismus

ALTERNATIVE: Functional movement disorder

ALTERNATIVE: Focal motor seizures with ictal choreiform movements
